summary: Defines how to wrap IPsec ESP packets inside UDP packets so they can pass through NAT devices, in both IPv4 and IPv6. The encapsulation is used when negotiated with IKE.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3948 defines how to carry IPsec ESP packets inside UDP packets so they can pass through Network Address Translators. IKE and ESP share UDP port use, while a marker distinguishes IKE packets from ESP packets.

questions: what is udp encapsulation of esp
why does ipsec nat-t use port 4500
subtitle: A packet format for carrying IPsec ESP inside UDP so it can cross Network Address Translators.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translators may not handle ESP packets because ESP is not TCP or UDP, so IPsec traffic can fail when a NAT is in the path.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3948 places ESP inside UDP using the ports used by IKE, defines a four-byte non-ESP marker to distinguish IKE, and defines a one-byte NAT keepalive packet.
tldr.outcome: When negotiated with IKE, UDP encapsulation lets ESP traverse NATs in IPv4 and IPv6 scenarios. Implementations must also handle conflicts when multiple clients share a NAT address.

today: RFC 3948 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005. It works with RFC 3947 for IKE negotiation; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Carry ESP in UDP
sections.content:
RFC 3948 defines how to encapsulate and decapsulate IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) packets inside UDP for traversal of Network Address Translators (NATs). The same UDP ports are used for IKE traffic, as specified by RFC 3947. Sharing the ports uses one NAT mapping, avoids separate IKE keepalives, and simplifies firewall configuration.

The method applies to IPv4 and IPv6 scenarios and is used when negotiated with IKE. It covers ESP, not IPsec Authentication Header (AH), because AH protects outer IP addresses that a NAT changes. Manual keying is not supported, and the ESP Security Parameter Index (SPI) MUST NOT be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT devices may not pass ESP directly. This RFC puts ESP inside UDP, which lets the traffic use the same port arrangement as IKE.

sections.title: UDP-Encapsulated ESP
sections.content:
A UDP-encapsulated ESP packet contains a standard UDP header followed by the ESP header and payload. The source and destination UDP ports MUST match those used by IKE traffic. For IPv4, the UDP checksum SHOULD be transmitted as zero, but receivers MUST NOT rely on it being zero. The ESP SPI field MUST NOT be zero.

The RFC describes packet formats using IPv4 headers, while stating that IPv6 can be used as either the outer or inner header.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet begins with a UDP header, then carries the ESP header and protected data. The ports match IKE, and the ESP SPI cannot be zero.

sections.title: Distinguishing IKE with the Non-ESP Marker
sections.content:
IKE packets sent on the shared UDP ports include a non-ESP marker between the UDP header and the IKE header. The marker is four zero-valued bytes. It aligns with the position of the ESP SPI field, which is required to be non-zero, so the receiver can distinguish IKE from ESP by examining the bytes after the UDP header.

The UDP header for IKE follows RFC 3947. RFC 3948 adds no new checksum requirements for IKE packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the first bytes after UDP. Four zero bytes mark IKE; an ESP packet cannot begin with a zero SPI.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
For transport mode, the sender applies ordinary ESP encapsulation, inserts a UDP header between the original IP header and ESP, and updates the IP packet's Total Length, Protocol, and IPv4 Header Checksum fields. The receiver removes the UDP header, updates the IP fields, performs ordinary ESP decapsulation, and applies the transport-mode NAT procedure.

For tunnel mode, UDP is inserted between the new outer IP header and ESP. The sender updates the new IP header fields. The receiver removes UDP, updates those fields, performs ESP decapsulation, and applies the tunnel-mode NAT procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender inserts UDP around ESP and updates the IP header fields to match. The receiver removes UDP, restores the corresponding header fields, and then processes ESP normally.

sections.title: Keeping NAT Mappings Alive
sections.content:
A NAT-keepalive packet exists only to keep a NAT mapping alive during a connection. It uses the same source and destination ports as UDP-encapsulated ESP and contains a one-octet payload with value 0xFF. The receiver SHOULD ignore the packet. Reception MUST NOT be used to decide whether the connection is live.

A peer MAY send keepalives while a phase I or phase II Security Association exists, or for a configurable period after one existed; the default is 5 minutes. When RFC 3947 indicates a keepalive is needed, a peer SHOULD send one if it has sent no other packet to the peer for the configurable idle time, whose default is 20 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-byte keepalive can prevent a NAT from expiring an idle mapping. It only preserves the mapping; it does not prove that the peer is reachable.

sections.title: Multiple Clients Behind One NAT
sections.content:
When two clients behind separate NATs use the same inner address to reach one security gateway in tunnel mode, the gateway may not know which client should receive return traffic. Implementations MUST prevent this conflict. The RFC recommends assigning locally unique addresses or translating client addresses to unique values.

In transport mode, two clients behind one NAT may have overlapping traffic descriptions. Implementations MUST handle ambiguity, for example by disallowing conflicting connections. A server cannot guarantee that one client behind a NAT uses IPsec while another sends the same traffic in clear text, because both can appear to come from the same address. Such a policy MUST NOT be used when security guarantees are required, though it MAY be used for best-effort security.
sections.plainLanguage: A server may see several clients behind a NAT as one address. Implementations must prevent return traffic and security policies from becoming ambiguous.
